passage:
I share a flat with Zubin, so I saw most of it.
In April his friend Rehan borrowed Zubin's motorbike and came back without it. "Stolen outside the cinema," he said. Two weeks later a mutual friend let slip that Rehan had crashed it and left it at a garage to avoid paying.
Zubin didn't shout. He went very quiet for days. He'd sit on the balcony in the evening with his tea going cold.
In June Rehan texted asking to meet. Zubin showed me the message and said, "I think I want to stop being angry. It's eating my evenings. But I'm not lending him anything ever again."
I asked if that meant they were friends again. He thought about it. "It means I'm putting it down. It doesn't mean I trust him."
He met Rehan for twenty minutes. He came home lighter, I think. I can't be sure. He still takes the bus.
Kavitha

qa.q: What had Rehan actually done with the motorbike?
qa.a: Rehan had crashed it and left it at a garage to avoid paying.

qa.q: What does Zubin mean by "putting it down"?
qa.a: Zubin wants to let go of the anger that is eating his evenings, without pretending the lie did not happen or trusting Rehan again.

qa.q: Which choice helps Zubin move forward without being hurt again?
qa.a: Deciding to release the resentment while refusing to lend Rehan anything again lets Zubin find peace and still protect himself.

qa.q: How might Rehan have felt meeting Zubin in June?
qa.a: Rehan may have hoped for full friendship again, and might have felt relief at Zubin's calm but also the limits Zubin kept.

grounding: Kavitha, who shares a flat with Zubin, watches him decide to let go of anger at a friend who lied, while making clear that forgiveness does not mean trusting him again.

passage:
Week one. Farhan found out from the internship list. Pema, who had sworn she wasn't applying so they wouldn't compete, had got the only place. He deleted her number, then un-deleted it, then lay awake composing messages he didn't send.
Week three. He was still angry, but tired of it. It came up during exams, on walks, while brushing his teeth. His Nani, on the phone, said, "Anger is like carrying a hot stone, beta. It burns the hand that holds it."
Week six. He met Pema at the college gate. She said sorry, properly. He listened.
"I'm not angry anymore," he told her. "I've let that go. But I don't think I'll share my plans with you for a long time."
She looked hurt. "So you haven't forgiven me."
"I have. Forgiving you is for me. Trusting you again is a different thing, and that part will take time."

qa.q: What did Farhan's Nani compare anger to?
qa.a: Farhan's Nani said anger is like carrying a hot stone that burns the hand that holds it.

qa.q: How did Farhan's feelings change between week one and week six?
qa.a: Farhan moved from sleepless anger to weariness of carrying it, and finally to a calm decision to let the resentment go.

qa.q: What turning point helped Farhan separate forgiving from trusting?
qa.a: Realising in week three that the anger was burning him, as his Nani said, helped him forgive for his own sake while keeping trust for later.

qa.q: How might Pema feel hearing that Farhan forgives her but won't share plans?
qa.a: Pema looked hurt and may feel the forgiveness is incomplete, since she hoped things would go back to how they were.

grounding: Over weeks Farhan, lied to by Pema, lets go of resentment without pretending nothing happened, and makes clear that forgiveness does not restore trust.

passage:
College counsellor's note, session 3, Dhruv (19)
Dhruv came in calmer today. Two months ago his close friend Nikita told the whole hostel floor about his father's job loss, after promising to keep it secret, and then denied it for weeks.
Today he said, "I'm tired of being angry. It's like carrying her bag everywhere." He wondered aloud if forgiving her meant pretending it never happened. I asked what he thought forgiveness was. After a long pause: "Maybe it's putting the bag down. And not giving her my secrets again."
He said he'd told Nikita, "I'm not angry anymore. But I'm not ready to tell you personal stuff." She cried. He said he felt sad and oddly light.
What I did next: I told him that letting go of anger and deciding how much to trust are two separate decisions, and both are his to make. We'll meet again in two weeks to see how the lighter feeling holds.

qa.q: What did Nikita tell the hostel floor?
qa.a: About his father's job loss, after promising to keep it secret.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel after speaking to Nikita?
qa.a: Dhruv felt sad and oddly light, having put down some of the anger without handing back his trust.

qa.q: What did the counsellor add that could help Dhruv?
qa.a: That letting go of anger and deciding how much to trust are separate decisions, both Dhruv's, with a check-in in two weeks.

qa.q: How might Nikita have felt when she heard Dhruv's words?
qa.a: Nikita cried, likely relieved the anger was fading but hurt that the closeness was not coming back.

grounding: Shows a young man who was lied to deciding that forgiveness means dropping the anger without pretending it didn't happen or restoring trust.

passage:
Sunday night
Saurabh finally admitted it today. He did take my bike that night, he did scrape it against the gate, and he let me blame the watchman's son for a week. The watchman's son! I shouted at a twelve-year-old because of him.
I've been angry for ten days. Waking up angry. It's exhausting.
Today, walking by the lake, I tried to work out what I actually want. I don't want to be his enemy for four years in the same flat. I don't want to keep replaying it. But I'm also not lending him anything again. Not the bike, not my notes, not my trust.
Maybe that's what forgiving is for me: I stop feeding the anger, but I don't pretend it didn't happen.
Told him that at dinner. He looked relieved, then a bit hurt at the second part. Fair.
Tomorrow I'm apologising to the watchman's son.
Gautam

qa.q: Who did Gautam blame for a week?
qa.a: The watchman's son.

qa.q: How had Gautam been feeling in the ten days before the admission?
qa.a: Gautam had been angry and exhausted, waking up angry and replaying it.

qa.q: What small step does Gautam plan for tomorrow, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Apologising to the watchman's son, who was wrongly blamed, which repairs a harm done while Gautam was angry.

qa.q: How did Saurabh react to Gautam's idea of forgiveness?
qa.a: Saurabh looked relieved at being forgiven, then a bit hurt that lending and trust were not coming back.

grounding: Shows a young adult deciding that forgiving a lying flatmate means letting go of anger without restoring trust or pretending it never happened.

passage: The ferry across the backwater was late, and Thomas sat on the jetty steps with Deepak's letter in his pocket. Last year Deepak had borrowed Thomas's motorbike for one wedding and returned it with a cracked engine casing, swearing a bus had hit it while parked. In January Thomas found out, from Deepak's own cousin, that Deepak had raced it on the canal road. The lie hurt more than the repair bill. For months Thomas replayed it every time he passed Deepak's house. Now Deepak had written: "I lied because I was scared. I'm sorry. I'll pay you back monthly." Thomas watched the water hyacinths drift. His Ammachi had told him forgiving didn't mean forgetting. He could let go of the anger that sat in his chest every morning; that was for himself. But lending the bike again? No. Trust would need time, and proof. When the ferry came, he texted Deepak: "I forgive you. Pay me back as you said. Let's see how it goes."

qa.q: What did Deepak claim had happened to the motorbike?
qa.a: That a bus had hit it while parked.

qa.q: How had Thomas felt for months after learning the truth?
qa.a: Thomas felt hurt and resentful, replaying the lie whenever he passed Deepak's house, with anger sitting in his chest every morning.

qa.q: How does Thomas separate forgiveness from trust?
qa.a: He lets go of the anger for his own peace and accepts the apology, but won't lend the bike again until time and repayment show change.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel reading Thomas's text?
qa.a: Deepak may feel relieved to be forgiven, but also aware that he must prove himself by paying back as promised.

grounding: Shows a young man lied to by a friend who chooses to release his resentment without pretending nothing happened or restoring full trust.
